Lastly, how great is the power and efficacy of faith is made known by this, that Christ so often declares in the Gospel: [[Mark 10:52|Thy faith hath made thee whole|Fides tua te salvum fecit]]; and, [[Mark 9:22|all things are possible to him that believeth|Omnia possibilia sunt credenti]]; and, [[Matt 17:19|if you have faith as a grain of mustard seed, you shall say to this mountain|Si habueritis fidem sicut granum sinapis, dicetis huic monti]]: [[Mark 11:23|Be thou removed and be cast into the sea|Tollere, et mittere in mare]], [[Matt 21:21|it shall be done|et fiet]]. Let us then be most certain and wholly immovable in the Catholic faith, which rests upon the divine authority and the truth of the uncreated Light. Paul uses this testimony just brought forward in writing to the Romans[[Rom 1:17||]] and to the Hebrews[[Heb 10:38||]].

paras.t: Consequenter ostendit Propheta, quod licet Deus ad tempus permittat impios prosperari, tacetque devorante impio justiorem se, nihilo minus tempore præstituto et congruo facit justam vindictam. Et hoc, quantum ad litteram, manifestatur jam in rege Babylonis: propter quod alii dicunt, Prophetam hoc loco ponere quæstionis superius motæ solutionem. Et quomodo vinum potantem decipit, id est, usu rationis privat et calore affligit, juxta illud: Blande ingreditur, sed in novissimo mordebit ut coluber. Hinc in Ecclesiastico habetur: Quam sufficiens est homini erudito vinum exiguum! et in dormiendo non laborabis ab illo, nec senties dolorem. Sic erit vir superbus, videlicet rex Babylonis. Quod aliqui referunt ad Nabuchodonosor, alii ad Balthasar ejus nepotem: tamen ut apparet, si littera rite pensetur, Propheta loquitur indeterminate de rege Babylonis, ita quod quædam referuntur ad Nabuchodonosor, quædam ad Balthasar. Quemadmodum ergo vinum decipit materialiter immoderate potantem, sic superbia regis Babylonis eum excæcavit, decepit, dejecit.
paras.en: Next the Prophet shows that although God for a time permits the wicked to prosper, and holds His peace when the wicked devours the man more just than himself, He nevertheless at the fitting time appointed takes just vengeance. And this, as to the letter, is now made plain in the king of Babylon; for which reason others say that the Prophet in this place gives the solution of the question raised above. [[2:5|And as wine deceiveth him that drinketh it|Et quomodo vinum potantem decipit]], that is, deprives him of the use of reason and afflicts him with heat, according to that saying: [[Prov 23:31|it goeth in pleasantly|Blande ingreditur]], [[Prov 23:32|But in the end, it will bite like a snake|sed in novissimo mordebit ut coluber]]. Hence it is said in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 31:22|How sufficient is a little wine for a man well taught, and in sleeping thou shalt not be uneasy with it, and thou shalt feel no pain.|Quam sufficiens est homini erudito vinum exiguum! et in dormiendo non laborabis ab illo, nec senties dolorem]] [[2:5|so shall the proud man be|Sic erit vir superbus]], namely the king of Babylon. Some refer this to Nabuchodonosor, others to Balthasar his grandson; yet, as appears if the letter is rightly weighed, the Prophet speaks of the king of Babylon without determining which, so that some things are referred to Nabuchodonosor, some to Balthasar. As then wine bodily deceives one who drinks immoderately, so pride blinded, deceived and cast down the king of Babylon.

paras.t: Et non decorabitur, id est, regio honore ac regno privabitur. Quod fuit absolute impletum in Balthasar, quem Persæ occiderunt ac Medi. Aliqualiter vero fuit impletum in Nabuchodonosor, quando (ut dictum est) factus est amens, et inter bestias conversatus, regno pulsus, fœnoque usus. Qui dilatavit quasi infernus animam suam, id est animæ suæ cupiditatem et crudelitatem, ita quod insatiabilis fuit sicut infernus. Quemadmodum enim infernus non impletur nec satiatur damnatis, sic rex Babylonis non satiabatur occisis atque divitiis, sed cuncta diripuit et vastavit. Et ipse quasi mors, propter suam crudelitatem amarus ut mors, nullique parcens; et non adimpletur cupiditas ejus: quum avarus semper sit egens, juxta quod scriptum est in Ecclesiaste: Avarus non implebitur pecunia. Et congregabit ad se omnes gentes, id est, gentes sibi viciniores suo imperio per violentiam subdet, et coacervabit ad se omnes populos, ut suo subjiciantur dominio. Istud præcipue competit Nabuchodonosor, qui regnum Babylonis maxime roboravit, et universa regna non nimis distantia debellavit. Propter quod scriptum est in Jeremia: Ab aquilone pandetur malum super omnem terram.
paras.en: [[2:5|and he shall not be honoured|Et non decorabitur]], that is, he will be deprived of royal honour and of the kingdom. This was fulfilled outright in Balthasar, whom the Persians and the Medes slew; and in some measure in Nabuchodonosor, when (as has been said) he was made mad, lived among the beasts, was driven from the kingdom and fed on hay. [[2:5|who hath enlarged his desire like hell|Qui dilatavit quasi infernus animam suam]] [the Latin has *animam suam*, "his soul"], that is, the greed and cruelty of his soul, so that he was insatiable like hell. For as hell is not filled nor sated with the damned, so the king of Babylon was not sated with the slain and with riches, but plundered and laid waste all things. [[2:5|and is himself like death|Et ipse quasi mors]], bitter as death because of his cruelty, and sparing none; [[2:5|and he is never satisfied|et non adimpletur cupiditas ejus]] [Denis adds *cupiditas ejus*, "his greed is not filled"]: since the covetous man is always in want, according to what is written in Ecclesiastes: [[Eccles 5:9|A covetous man shall not be satisfied with money|Avarus non implebitur pecunia]]. [[2:5|but will gather together unto him all nations|Et congregabit ad se omnes gentes]], that is, he will subject by violence to his rule the nations nearer to him, [[2:5|and heap together unto him all people|et coacervabit ad se omnes populos]], that they may be made subject to his dominion. This fits Nabuchodonosor above all, who greatly strengthened the kingdom of Babylon and subdued all the kingdoms not too far distant. For which reason it is written in Jeremias: [[Jer 1:14|From the north shall an evil break forth|Ab aquilone pandetur malum]] upon all the earth [Denis has *super omnem terram*, "upon all the earth"; the Vulgate reads "upon all the inhabitants of the land"].

paras.t: Numquid non omnes isti, id est populi a rege Babylonis vastati, super eum sument parabolam, id est, proverbium de eo et ejus dejectione formabunt, et loquelam ænigmatum ejus, id est verbum figuralium difficultatem seu parabolicarum obscuritatem de rege nunc dicto? et dicetur: Væ ei qui multiplicat non sua, id est, debita pœna modo inflicta est regi Babylonio alios spolianti. Usquequo aggravat contra se, id est, in malum animæ suæ auget, et onere violentarum prædarum colligit, densum lutum, id est terrenas divitias ad vitia graviter deprimentes, quæ affectum in infimis mergunt, ne queat ad superna levari? Denique aurum et argentum quid nisi terra alba et rubea? Et sicut magna est vilitas luti, sic temporales divitiæ a spiritualibus viris vilipenduntur, qui cum Paulo omnia arbitrantur ut stercora, ut Christum lucrifaciant. Denique ista partim impleta sunt in Nabuchodonosor tempore suæ amentiæ, qui tunc a populis irridebatur. In Balthasar vero impleta sunt absolute, quando a Medis occisus est. Cui consequenter ait Propheta:
paras.en: [[2:6|Shall not all these|Numquid non omnes isti]], that is, the peoples laid waste by the king of Babylon, [[2:6|take up a parable against him|super eum sument parabolam]], that is, make a proverb about him and his overthrow, [[2:6|and a dark speech concerning him|et loquelam ænigmatum ejus]] [literally "the speech of his riddles"], that is, a word full of the difficulty of figures, or the obscurity of parables, about the king just spoken of? [[2:6|and it shall be said: Woe to him that heapeth together that which is not his own?|et dicetur: Væ ei qui multiplicat non sua]], that is, a due punishment has now been laid upon the Babylonian king who despoiled others. [[2:6|how long also doth he load himself|Usquequo aggravat contra se]], that is, he heaps up to the harm of his soul and gathers with the burden of violent plunder, [[2:6|with thick clay|densum lutum]], that is, earthly riches, which weigh men down heavily to vices, and sink the affections in the lowest things, so that they cannot be raised to things above? Indeed, what are gold and silver but white and red earth? And as the vileness of clay is great, so temporal riches are held cheap by spiritual men, who with Paul [[Phil 3:8|count them but as dung, that I may gain Christ|omnia arbitrantur ut stercora, ut Christum lucrifaciant]] [Denis has "that they may gain Christ"]. These things were partly fulfilled in Nabuchodonosor at the time of his madness, when he was mocked by the peoples; but in Balthasar they were fulfilled outright, when he was slain by the Medes. To whom the Prophet next says:

paras.t: Numquid non repente consurgent qui mordeant te? id est, imo cito te impugnabunt Cyrus ac Darius cum exercitibus suis Medis Persisque. Et suscitabuntur lacerantes te, id est, civitatem et populum tuum destruentes, teque occidentes, et evigilabunt insidiatores tui, id est, diligenter te obsidebunt Medi et Persæ, et eris in rapinam eis, id est, bona tua diripient.
paras.en: [[2:7|Shall they not rise up suddenly that shall bite thee|Numquid non repente consurgent qui mordeant te]]? that is, nay, Cyrus and Darius with their armies of Medes and Persians will soon attack thee. [[2:7|and they be stirred up that shall tear thee|Et suscitabuntur lacerantes te]], that is, destroying thy city and thy people, and slaying thee, and they that lie in wait for thee shall awake [these words, *et evigilabunt insidiatores tui*, are not in the Vulgate text of the verse], that is, the Medes and Persians will besiege thee diligently, [[2:7|and thou shalt be a spoil to them|et eris in rapinam eis]], that is, they will plunder thy goods.

paras.t: Quia tu spoliasti gentes multas, spoliabunt te omnes qui reliqui fuerint de populis: id est, gentes quæ manus tuas evaserunt, jungent se hostibus tuis, et simul cum illis rapient tuas divitias; fietque tibi sicut fecisti in alios. Distributiones vero hic positæ, arctandæ sunt secundum subjectam materiam, et accipiendæ pro generibus singulorum, potius quam pro singulis generum. Hæc autem potissime patieris, rex Babylonis, propter sanguinem hominis, id est occisionem hominum Judæorum, et iniquitatem terræ civitatis, id est peccata quæ commisisti contra Judæam, in qua est civitas Jerusalem famosa ac metropolitana, et hominum habitantium in ea, id est propter peccata quæ in habitatores Jerusalem perpetrasti, quos crudeliter oppressisti. Quamvis autem rex Babylonis dire peccavit, alias nationes vastando, gravius tamen peccavit, populum Judæorum ac templum demoliendo. Idcirco propter illorum occisionem præsertim, dejectus asseritur.
paras.en: [[2:8|Because thou hast spoiled many nations, all that shall be left of the people|Quia tu spoliasti gentes multas, spoliabunt te omnes qui reliqui fuerint de populis]]: that is, the nations that escaped thy hands will join themselves to thy enemies, and together with them will seize thy riches; and it will be done to thee as thou didst to others. But the universal words set down here [*all that shall be left*] are to be narrowed according to the subject matter, and taken for some of every kind rather than for every one of each kind [that is, the scholastic distinction *pro generibus singulorum*, not *pro singulis generum*]. And these things thou shalt suffer most of all, O king of Babylon, [[2:8|because of men's blood|propter sanguinem hominis]], that is, for the slaughter of the Jews, [[2:8|and for the iniquity of the land, of the city|et iniquitatem terræ civitatis]], that is, the sins thou hast committed against Judea, in which is the city of Jerusalem, renowned and the mother city, [[2:8|and of all that dwell therein|et hominum habitantium in ea]], that is, for the sins thou hast wrought against the inhabitants of Jerusalem, whom thou hast cruelly oppressed. For although the king of Babylon sinned grievously in laying waste other nations, yet he sinned more gravely in destroying the people of the Jews and the temple. Therefore it is above all for their slaughter that he is said to have been cast down.

paras.t: Væ regi Babylonis, qui congregat avaritiam, id est materiam avaritiæ, scilicet bona terrena, malam domui suæ, id est sibi et filiis atque familiis suis nocivam, ut sit in excelso nidus ejus, id est, palatium et habitatio ejus, seu Babylon civitas ejus, sit in magna eminentia, potestate et gloria, et liberari se putat de manu mali, id est de potestate hostili et malo pœnali. De hoc nido dixit Nabuchodonosor: Nonne hæc est Babylon civitas magna, quam ædificavi in domum regni, in robore fortitudinis meæ, et in gloria decoris mei?
paras.en: [[2:9|Woe|Væ]] to the king of Babylon, [[2:9|that gathereth together|qui congregat]] [[2:9|covetousness|avaritiam]], that is, the stuff of covetousness, namely earthly goods, [[2:9|an evil|malam]] [[2:9|to his house|domui suæ]], that is, harmful to himself and to his sons and households, [[2:9|that his nest may be on high|ut sit in excelso nidus ejus]], that is, that his palace and dwelling, or Babylon his city, may be in great eminence, power and glory, [[2:9|and thinketh he may be delivered out of the hand of evil|et liberari se putat de manu mali]], that is, from hostile power and from the evil of punishment. Of this nest Nabuchodonosor said: [[Dan 4:27|Is not this the great Babylon, which I have built, to be the seat of the kingdom, by the strength of my power, and in the glory of my excellence?|Nonne hæc est Babylon civitas magna, quam ædificavi in domum regni, in robore fortitudinis meæ, et in gloria decoris mei?]]

paras.t: Cogitasti confusionem, id est causam confusionis, domui tuæ: hoc est, tua cogitatione iniqua atque superba meruisti posteros tuos et regnum confundi atque superari: secundum quod Deus iniquitatem patrum visitat in tertiam et quartam generationem. Nam propter peccata parentum ac principum, filii et subjecti aliquando corporalibus pœnis afficiuntur. Et concidisti populos multos, vulnerando, prædando seu occidendo, et peccavit anima tua.
paras.en: [[2:10|Thou hast devised confusion|Cogitasti confusionem]], that is, the cause of confusion, [[2:10|to thy house|domui tuæ]]: that is, by thy wicked and proud thinking thou hast deserved that thy descendants and thy kingdom be confounded and overcome; according as God visits [[Ex 20:5|the iniquity of the fathers|iniquitatem patrum]] [[Ex 20:5|unto the third and fourth generation|in tertiam et quartam generationem]]. For because of the sins of parents and princes, children and subjects are sometimes afflicted with bodily punishments. [[2:10|thou hast cut off many people|concidisti populos multos]], by wounding, plundering or slaying, [[2:10|and thy soul hath sinned|et peccavit anima tua]].

paras.t: Cujus signum est: Quia lapis de pariete clamabit, et lignum quod inter juncturas ædificiorum est, respondebit: id est, lapides parietum a te destructorum materialium, adversus te conclamabunt, quoniam sua ruina ac dissipatione ostendent tuam crudelitatem, et dabunt hominibus occasionem atque materiam clamandi et ultionem appetendi de te. Simili modo ligna quibus partes ædificiorum connectuntur, materialiter respondebunt, id est, quærentibus ostendent causam tuæ destructionis: quoniam tanta fuit severitas tua in ædificiorum alienorum dissipatione, quod nidus tuus seu Babylon est destructa. Inanimata itaque materialiter dicuntur clamare et respondere, sicut in Psalmis dicuntur laudare et benedicere, juxta illud: Valles abundabunt frumento; clamabunt, etenim hymnum dicent.
paras.en: The sign of which is: [[2:11|For the stone shall cry out of the wall: and the timber that is between the joints of the building, shall answer|Quia lapis de pariete clamabit, et lignum quod inter juncturas ædificiorum est, respondebit]]: that is, the stones of the material walls destroyed by thee will cry out together against thee, since by their ruin and scattering they will show thy cruelty, and will give men occasion and matter for crying out and for seeking vengeance on thee. In like manner the timbers by which the parts of buildings are joined will answer materially, that is, will show those who ask the cause of thy destruction: since so great was thy severity in pulling down the buildings of others, that thy nest, that is, Babylon, has been destroyed. Thus inanimate things are said, in a material sense, to cry out and to answer, as in the Psalms they are said to praise and to bless[[Ps 148:3||]][[Dan 3:57||]], according to that saying: [[Ps 64:14|the vales shall abound with corn: they shall shout, yea they shall sing a hymn|Valles abundabunt frumento; clamabunt, etenim hymnum dicent]].

paras.t: Adhuc Propheta invehitur contra Nabuchodonosor. Væ qui ædificat civitatem in sanguinibus, id est, Babylonem construxit in magnis peccatis et homicidiis, interficiens populos, ut de prædis eorum urbem suam construeret. Idcirco subjungitur: et præparat urbem jam dictam in iniquitate, id est de sumptibus injuste adeptis atque in maxima pompa.
paras.en: The Prophet further inveighs against Nabuchodonosor. [[2:12|Woe to him that buildeth a town with blood|Væ qui ædificat civitatem in sanguinibus]], that is, he built Babylon in great sins and murders, slaying peoples, that from their spoils he might build his city. Therefore it is added: [[2:12|and prepareth a city|et præparat urbem]], the one already spoken of, [[2:12|by iniquity|in iniquitate]], that is, from means unjustly gained, and in the greatest pomp.

paras.t: Numquid non hæc sunt a Domino exercituum? id est, nonne subscriptæ vindictæ a Deo infligentur regi et populo Babylonis? tanquam dicat, Utique. Laborabunt enim populi, id est Babylonii, in multo igne, id est ad impediendum vel exstinguendum Babylonis incendium; et gentes Chaldaicæ in vacuum laborabunt, defendendo se contra Persas et Medos, et deficient Babylonii seu Chaldæi, non valentes Medis et Persis resistere.
paras.en: [[2:13|Are not these things from the Lord of hosts|Numquid non hæc sunt a Domino exercituum]]? that is, will not the punishments written below be inflicted by God on the king and people of Babylon? as if to say: Assuredly. [[2:13|for the people shall labour|Laborabunt enim populi]], that is, the Babylonians, [[2:13|in a great fire|in multo igne]], that is, to check or put out the burning of Babylon; [[2:13|and the nations|et gentes]] of the Chaldeans shall labour [[2:13|in vain|in vacuum]], defending themselves against the Persians and Medes, [[2:13|and they shall faint|et deficient]], the Babylonians or Chaldeans, not being able to withstand the Medes and Persians.

paras.t: Quia replebitur terra, id est Chaldæa hostibus nunc sæpe expressis, ut cognoscat gloriam Domini: id est, ipsi Chaldæi per suæ vastitatis angustiam experimentaliter sentiunt vel cognoscent excellentiam potestatis divinæ, cujus virtute viderint se superari, quemadmodum Daniel prædixerat Balthasar regi. Hæc autem repletio terræ, et experimentalis agnitio gloriæ Domini, fuit plurimum copiosa, quasi aquæ operientes mare.
paras.en: [[2:14|For the earth shall be filled|Quia replebitur terra]], that is, Chaldea, with the enemies now often named, [[2:14|that men may know the glory of the Lord|ut cognoscat gloriam Domini]]: that is, the Chaldeans themselves, through the distress of their devastation, feel or will know by experience the excellence of the divine power, by whose might they will see themselves overcome, as Daniel had foretold to king Balthasar[[Dan 5:18||]]. And this filling of the earth and experiential knowledge of the glory of the Lord was most abundant, [[2:14|as waters covering the sea|quasi aquæ operientes mare]].

paras.t: Væ qui potum dat amico suo, mittens fel suum, id est, fel potui miscens, et felleum potum exhibens, et inebrians, id est tali potu fraudulenter immoderateque implens potantem, ut adspiciat nuditatem ejus, id est verecundiam, ignominiam, paupertatem. Istud ad litteram contra Nabuchodonosor dicitur, de quo ferunt Hebræi, quod quum in Babylone magnum convivium faceret, jussit Sedeciam regem Juda adduci, et potu laxativo potari: quo facto, Sedecias mox coram omnibus passus est ventris fluxum, unde post paucum præ confusione et dolore defunctus est. Istud tamen secundum Hieronymum et Bedam, potius est fabula quam res vera.
paras.en: [[2:15|Woe to him that giveth drink to his friend|Væ qui potum dat amico suo]], [[2:15|and presenteth his gall|mittens fel suum]], that is, mixing gall in the drink and offering a drink of gall, [[2:15|and maketh him drunk|et inebrians]], that is, filling the drinker with such a drink deceitfully and beyond measure, [[2:15|that he may behold his nakedness|ut adspiciat nuditatem ejus]], that is, his shame, disgrace and poverty. This is said literally against Nabuchodonosor, of whom the Hebrews relate that when he was giving a great banquet in Babylon, he ordered Sedecias king of Juda to be brought in and given a purging drink; whereupon Sedecias soon suffered a flux of the bowels before them all, and from this a little later died of shame and pain. But according to Jerome and Bede this is rather a fable than a true thing.

paras.t: Ideo exponunt communiter, ut sit sensus: Væ regi Babylonis præfato, qui potum, id est afflictionem, dat amico suo, id est proximis, vel his quibus aliquando confœderatus fuit, seu ei amicabiles fuerunt. Et hoc modo Sedecias fuit amicus ejus, quando ad tempus ei servivit, et fœdus servavit quod iniit, quando Nabuchodonosor constituit eum regem. Mittens fel suum, id est, cordis sui amaritudinem, severitatem, fallaciam ducens ad actum, et inebrians, id est, abundanter adimplens potantes, hoc modo, ut adspiciat nuditatem ejus, id est, alios omnes spoliatos et depauperatos ac victos conspiceret. Ad hoc quippe omnia regna vastavit et spoliavit, ut suam potentiam decoraret, et comparatione nuditatis illorum, sua opulentia gloriosior videretur.
paras.en: Therefore they commonly expound it so that the sense is: Woe to the aforesaid king of Babylon, who gives drink, that is, affliction, to his friend, that is, to his neighbours, or to those with whom he was at some time in league, or who were friendly to him. And in this way Sedecias was his friend, when for a time he served him and kept the covenant he had made when Nabuchodonosor made him king[[4 Kings 24:17||]]. [[2:15|and presenteth his gall|Mittens fel suum]], that is, carrying into act the bitterness, severity and guile of his heart, [[2:15|and maketh him drunk|et inebrians]], that is, filling the drinkers abundantly, in this way, [[2:15|that he may behold his nakedness|ut adspiciat nuditatem ejus]], that is, that he might look upon all others despoiled, impoverished and conquered. For to this end he laid waste and despoiled all kingdoms, that he might adorn his own power, and that by comparison with their nakedness his own wealth might seem the more glorious.

paras.t: Repletus est ignominia, id est, Sedecias, seu alius quilibet a rege Babylonis prædicto modo potatus et inebriatus, magnam consecutus est calamitatem et confusionem, pro gloria, id est honore regio, vel alia quacumque eminentia, potestate, vel abundantia, qua floruit in hoc mundo. Bibe tu quoque, et consopire, id est, o rex Babylonis, sicut fecisti, fiet tibi: bibes enim calicem tribulationis, et afflictione velut potu impleberis atque deficies. Quod referri potest ad Nabuchodonosor, quantum ad punitionem ejus sibi in hoc mundo inflictam, quando in amentiam versus est; vel ad filium filii sui, puta ad Balthasar regem, a Medis et Persis occisum. Ad utrumque etiam potest pertinere quod subditur: Circumdabit te calix dexteræ Domini, id est magna punitio a divina virtute pro ultione inflicta, et vomitus ignominiæ circumdabit te, ut egeras quæ absorbuisti, aliis ea relinquendo, scilicet spolia, super gloriam tuam, id est post magnificentiam imperii tui; vel tibi adhuc regnanti ista contingent. Vel per vomitum ignominiæ designatur superabundans calamitas, quæ ad instar immoderatissimæ potionis erumpit.
paras.en: [[2:16|Thou art filled with shame|Repletus est ignominia]] [Denis reads *Repletus est*, "he is filled", and takes it of Sedecias], that is, Sedecias, or anyone else given drink and made drunk by the king of Babylon in the way described, met with great calamity and confusion, [[2:16|instead of glory|pro gloria]], that is, of royal honour, or of whatever other eminence, power or abundance in which he flourished in this world. [[2:16|drink thou also, and fall fast asleep|Bibe tu quoque, et consopire]], that is, O king of Babylon, as thou hast done, so shall it be done to thee: for thou shalt drink the cup of tribulation, and be filled with affliction as with drink, and faint. This can be referred to Nabuchodonosor, as to the punishment laid on him in this world when he was turned to madness[[Dan 4:30||]]; or to his son's son, namely king Balthasar, slain by the Medes and Persians[[Dan 5:30||]]. To both also can belong what follows: [[2:16|the cup of the right hand of the Lord shall compass thee|Circumdabit te calix dexteræ Domini]], that is, a great punishment inflicted by the divine power in vengeance, [[2:16|and shameful vomiting|et vomitus ignominiæ]] shall compass thee, so that thou mayest bring up what thou hast swallowed, leaving it to others, namely the spoils, [[2:16|shall be on thy glory|super gloriam tuam]], that is, after the magnificence of thy empire; or these things will befall thee while thou art still reigning. Or by the vomiting of shame is meant an overflowing calamity, which bursts forth like a most immoderate draught.

paras.t: Quia iniquitas Libani, id est peccatum quod commisisti in templum Dei in Jerusalem, illud profanando ac destruendo, operiet te: id est, propter illud graviter punieris. Dicitur autem templum, Libanus, quia de lignis Libani fuit constructum, ut legitur tertio libro Regum. Propter quod in Zacharia habetur: Aperi, Libane, portas tuas. Et vastitas animalium, id est devastatio sacrificiorum, quæ de animalibus offerebantur in templo, deterrebit eos, id est, causa erit quod Babylonii seu Chaldæi a suis adversariis terrebuntur: meruerunt enim interfici a Persis hoc faciendo; de sanguinibus hominis, id est etiam pro effusione sanguinis Judæorum; et iniquitate terræ, id est crudelitate et pravitate, quam in terra Juda commiserunt, et civitatis Jerusalem et omnium habitantium in ea. Chaldæi itaque propter peccata commissa in Deum, cujus cultum et templum demoliti sunt, atque in populum ejus, quem in Jerusalem ac Judæa atrociter vexaverunt, a Deo plagati, et hostibus traditi sunt.
paras.en: [[2:17|For the iniquity of Libanus|Quia iniquitas Libani]], that is, the sin thou didst commit against the temple of God in Jerusalem, profaning and destroying it, [[2:17|shall cover thee|operiet te]]: that is, for it thou shalt be grievously punished. Now the temple is called Libanus because it was built of the timber of Libanus, as we read in the third book of Kings[[3 Kings 5:6||]] [the margin gives III Reg. v, 5 and following]. For which reason it is said in Zacharias: [[Zach 11:1|Open thy gates, O Libanus|Aperi, Libane, portas tuas]]. [[2:17|and the ravaging of beasts|Et vastitas animalium]], that is, the laying waste of the sacrifices which were offered from animals in the temple, [[2:17|shall terrify them|deterrebit eos]], that is, will be the cause why the Babylonians or Chaldeans will be terrified by their adversaries: for by doing this they deserved to be slain by the Persians; [[2:17|because of the blood of men|de sanguinibus hominis]], that is, for the shedding of the blood of the Jews too; [[2:17|and the iniquity of the land|et iniquitate terræ]], that is, the cruelty and wickedness they committed in the land of Juda, [[2:17|and of the city|et civitatis]] of Jerusalem, [[2:17|and of all that dwell therein|et omnium habitantium in ea]]. Thus the Chaldeans, for the sins committed against God, whose worship and temple they destroyed, and against His people, whom they cruelly harassed in Jerusalem and Judea, were stricken by God and handed over to their enemies[[4 Kings 25:1||]].

paras.t: Consequenter contra omnes idololatras, specialiter tamen ac litteraliter contra Nabuchodonosor, dicitur: Quid prodest sculptile, id est idolum sculptum, quia sculpsit illud fictor suus, id est, formator illud artificiose formavit, ornavit et figuravit? tanquam dicat: Quum sculptile sit ab homine factum, constat quod prodesse non queat, nec aliquid virtutis aut numinis habeat. Et conflatile, id est idolum conflatum, quid prodest, quod fictor suus fecit, et imaginem falsam molitus est? Idolum namque est falsa imago, quoniam decipit, nec id quod repræsentat, tale est quale per idolum significatur. Imo secundum Apostolum, idolum nihil est, scilicet quantum ad repræsentatum.
paras.en: Next it is said against all idolaters, but specially and literally against Nabuchodonosor: [[2:18|What doth the graven thing avail|Quid prodest sculptile]], that is, the carved idol, [[2:18|because the maker thereof hath graven it|quia sculpsit illud fictor suus]], that is, the fashioner has skilfully formed, adorned and shaped it? as if to say: since the graven thing is made by man, it is plain that it can profit nothing, nor has it any power or divinity. [[2:18|a molten|Et conflatile]], that is, a cast idol, what does it profit, which its maker made, [[2:18|and a false image|et imaginem falsam]] that he fashioned? For an idol is a false image, since it deceives, and what it represents is not such as is signified by the idol. Nay rather, according to the Apostle, [[1 Cor 8:4|an idol is nothing|idolum nihil est]], namely as to what it represents.

paras.t: Inter sculptile et conflatile hoc distat, secundum Bedam, quod sculptile est de ligno aut marmore, conflatile de metallo. Tamen, ut alii dicunt, idem potest esse sculptile atque conflatile: quod enim igne conflatum est, potest postea arte sculptoria aptius figurari, quemadmodum factum affirmant de vitulo aureo in deserto a filiis Israel facto, qui erat conflatilis, et etiam sculptilis, juxta illud in Psalmo: Et fecerunt vitulum in Horeb, et adoraverunt sculptile.
paras.en: Between the graven and the molten thing there is this difference, according to Bede: that the graven thing is of wood or marble, the molten of metal. Yet, as others say, the same thing can be both graven and molten: for what has been cast in the fire can afterwards be shaped more fitly by the sculptor's art, as they affirm was done with the golden calf made by the children of Israel in the desert[[Ex 32:4||]], which was molten and also graven, according to that in the Psalm: [[Ps 105:19|They made also a calf in Horeb: and they adored the graven thing|Et fecerunt vitulum in Horeb, et adoraverunt sculptile]].

paras.t: Quia speravit in figmento, id est idolo, fictor ejus, vel qui jussit illud formari, vel qui opere adimplevit, ut faceret simulacra muta, id est idola inanimata aurea atque argentea. Quidam exponunt hæc de statua aurea quam Nabuchodonosor fecit atque erexit in campo Duran; in qua fecit se adorari, ut dicunt. Alii vero dicunt, quod de statua illa non sit jam sermo, quia in ea Nabuchodonosor non confidebat, sed in aliis idolis quæ colebat. Nihilo minus de statua illa accipi potest quod de sculptili atque conflatili dictum est. De idolis vero quæ coluit Nabuchodonosor, sumi potest quod de simulacris mutis adjectum est.
paras.en: [[2:18|because the forger thereof hath trusted in a thing of his own forging|Quia speravit in figmento]], that is, in the idol; the forger being either he who ordered it to be formed or he who carried out the work, [[2:18|to make dumb idols|ut faceret simulacra muta]], that is, lifeless idols of gold and silver. Some expound these words of the golden statue which Nabuchodonosor made and set up in the plain of Duran[[Dan 3:1||]], in which he had himself adored, as they say. But others say that that statue is not spoken of here, because Nabuchodonosor did not trust in it, but in other idols which he worshipped. Nevertheless, what is said of the graven and the molten thing can be taken of that statue; and what is added about dumb idols can be taken of the idols that Nabuchodonosor worshipped.

paras.t: Væ æternæ damnationis, nisi pœniteat, imminet ei qui dicit ligno, id est idolo ligneo, Expergiscere, id est, evigila ad adjuvandum seu instruendum me, et qui dicit, Surge, lapidi tacenti, id est idolo lapideo, quod loqui non potest. Numquid ipse lapis, seu deus lapideus, docere poterit, id est futura prædicere, occulta revelare, dubia determinare? Istud specialiter contra regem Babylonis inducitur; sed accipi potest contra omnes idololatras, qui idola lignea atque lapidea invocant. Ecce iste, id est lapis, seu deus lapideus, coopertus est auro et argento, id est pretiosis ornamentis circumtextus, vel deauratus, aut argento circumdatus; et omnis spiritus non est in visceribus ejus, id est, spiritum vitalem nullum intra se habet pro forma, imo nec veraciter viscera habet, sicut nec oculos, aures, aut manus, sed similitudinem tantum, seu apparentiam.
paras.en: [[2:19|Woe|Væ]] of eternal damnation, unless he repent, hangs over [[2:19|him that saith to wood|ei qui dicit ligno]], that is, to a wooden idol: [[2:19|Awake|Expergiscere]], that is, wake up to help or instruct me; and over him who says [[2:19|Arise|Surge]] [[2:19|to the dumb stone|lapidi tacenti]], that is, to a stone idol, which cannot speak[[Ps 113:13||]] [the margin gives Ps. cxiii, 5, according to the Hebrew, that is, Psalm 115:5 in the Hebrew numbering, the second part of Psalm 113 in the Vulgate]. [[2:19|can it|Numquid ipse]], the stone itself, or the stone god, [[2:19|teach|docere poterit]], that is, foretell things to come, reveal hidden things, settle doubtful ones? This is brought in specially against the king of Babylon, but it can be taken against all idolaters who call upon idols of wood and stone. [[2:19|Behold, it|Ecce iste]], that is, the stone, or the stone god, [[2:19|is laid over with gold, and silver|coopertus est auro et argento]], that is, clothed round with precious ornaments, or gilded, or overlaid with silver; [[2:19|and there is no spirit in the bowels thereof|et omnis spiritus non est in visceribus ejus]], that is, it has no living spirit within it for its form; nay, it has not truly any bowels, as neither eyes, ears nor hands[[Ps 113:13||]][[Ps 113:14||]][[Ps 113:15||]], but only their likeness or appearance [the margin gives Ps. cxiii, 5–7, again by the Hebrew numbering: Vulgate Ps 113:13–15].

paras.t: Dominus autem in templo sancto suo, id est, Deus verus atque omnipotens, non in idolis vel idololatris, sed in electis et sanctis per gratiam, et in Beatis seu comprehensoribus per gloriam, in cœlo quoque empyreo per suæ majestatis evidentiorem repræsentationem, suæque potestatis eminentiorem operationem, est atque moratur. Sileat a facie ejus omnis terra, id est, omnis homo in terra habitans, consideratione majestatis divinæ humilietur, et a verbis idololatriæ atque blasphemiæ cesset, nec aliquid contra Deum loqui præsumat, sed timore illius ori suo ponat custodiam.
paras.en: [[2:20|But the Lord is in his holy temple|Dominus autem in templo sancto suo]], that is, the true and almighty God is and abides, not in idols or idolaters, but in the elect and the saints by grace, and in the Blessed or comprehensors [that is, those who already possess God in the vision of glory, as opposed to wayfarers] by glory, and in the empyrean heaven too by a more evident showing of His majesty and a more eminent working of His power. [[2:20|let all the earth keep silence before him|Sileat a facie ejus omnis terra]], that is, let every man dwelling on the earth be humbled by considering the divine majesty, and cease from words of idolatry and blasphemy, and not presume to say anything against God, but out of fear of Him set a watch upon his mouth[[Ps 140:3||]].

2.title: Explanatio moralis ejusdem secundi capituli.
2.title_en: Moral explanation of the same second chapter.

paras.t: Quilibet insuper veraciter christianus dicere habet: Super custodiam meam stabo, id est, tota vigilantia mentis insistam custodiæ cordis mei, ut illud in puritate conservem, et Deo habitaculum dignum exhibeam, exemplo ejus qui ait: Dixi, Custodiam vias meas. Ideo Salomon: Omni, inquit, custodia custodi cor tuum, quia ex ipso vita procedit. Et Ecclesiasticus ait: Si non in timore Domini tenueris te instanter, cito subvertetur domus tua. Hinc in Deuteronomio Moyses exhortatur: Custodi temetipsum et animam tuam sollicite; et ne obliviscaris verborum Domini Dei tui, et ne excidant de corde tuo cunctis diebus vitæ tuæ. Puritas enim cordis, quæ aliud non est nisi contemplativa atque sincera delectatio, seu delectativa et munda contemplatio Dei, est finis omnium exercitiorum nostrorum: ob quam exteriores sensus et linguam ac ventrem frenamus. Propterea jugiter occupari oportet pro cordis munditia obtinenda, conservanda, ac consummanda: quod qui faciunt, audiunt a Salvatore: Beati mundo corde, quoniam ipsi Deum videbunt. Sic utique stetit super custodiam suam sanctus Job, dicens: Considerans Deum, timore sollicitor; et item, Semper quasi tumentes super me fluctus timui Deum. Elias quoque et Eliseus, dicentes: Vivit Dominus, in cujus conspectu sto hodie. Consideratio nempe divinæ præsentiæ maxime confert ad istam custodiam. Propter quod ait Psalmista: Servavi mandata tua et testimonia tua, quia omnes viæ meæ in conspectu tuo. Horum itaque imitemur vestigia, ut impleamus quod docet Apostolus ad Philippenses: Cum metu et tremore vestram salutem operamini.
paras.en: Moreover every true Christian has to say: [[2:1|I will stand upon my watch|Super custodiam meam stabo]], that is, with all the watchfulness of my mind I will apply myself to the keeping of my heart, so as to preserve it in purity and offer God a worthy dwelling, after the example of him who says: [[Ps 38:2|I said: I will take heed to my ways|Dixi, Custodiam vias meas]] [the margin gives Ps. xxxvii, 2; the words are Ps 38:2]. Therefore Solomon says: [[Prov 4:23|With all watchfulness|Omni]], he says, [[Prov 4:23|keep thy heart, because life issueth out from it|custodia custodi cor tuum, quia ex ipso vita procedit]]. And Ecclesiasticus says: [[Ecclus 27:4|Unless thou hold thyself diligently in the fear of the Lord, thy house shall quickly be overthrown.|Si non in timore Domini tenueris te instanter, cito subvertetur domus tua.]] Hence in Deuteronomy Moses exhorts: [[Deut 4:9|Keep thyself therefore, and thy soul carefully|Custodi temetipsum et animam tuam sollicite]]; [[Deut 4:9|Forget not the words|et ne obliviscaris verborum]] of the Lord thy God, [[Deut 4:9|and let them not go out of thy heart all the days of thy life|et ne excidant de corde tuo cunctis diebus vitæ tuæ]]. For purity of heart, which is nothing else than a contemplative and sincere delight in God, or a delighting and clean contemplation of God, is the end of all our exercises: it is for its sake that we bridle the outward senses, the tongue and the belly. Therefore we must be busied continually with obtaining, preserving and perfecting cleanness of heart; and those who do so hear from the Saviour: [[Matt 5:8|Blessed are the clean of heart: they shall see God.|Beati mundo corde: quoniam ipsi Deum videbunt.]] So indeed did holy Job stand upon his watch, saying: [[Job 23:15|when I consider him, I am made pensive with fear|Considerans Deum, timore sollicitor]]; and again, [[Job 31:23|I have always feared God as waves swelling over me|Semper quasi tumentes super me fluctus timui Deum]]. So too Elias and Eliseus, saying: [[3 Kings 17:1|As the Lord liveth|Vivit Dominus]], [[3 Kings 17:1|in whose sight I stand|in cujus conspectu sto]] this day[[4 Kings 3:14||]]. For the consideration of the divine presence helps most of all towards this watch. Wherefore the Psalmist says: [[Ps 118:168|I have kept thy commandments and thy testimonies: because all my ways are in thy sight.|Servavi mandata tua et testimonia tua, quia omnes viæ meæ in conspectu tuo.]] Let us therefore follow in their footsteps, that we may fulfil what the Apostle teaches the Philippians: [[Phil 2:12|with fear and trembling work out your salvation|Cum metu et tremore vestram salutem operamini]].

paras.t: Et figam gradum, id est, incessum cordis seu actum stabiliam, firmiterque locabo, super munitionem, id est animæ armaturam, confortationem ac defensionem, ut sim semper sollicitus animam habere munitam, ne ab hostibus suæ salutis vincatur, ne peccatis aut passionibus superetur. Ideo enim monet Apostolus ad Ephesios: Induite vos armaturam Dei ut possitis stare adversus insidias diaboli. Vel, Figam gradum super munitionem, id est Christum, de quo legitur in Isaia: Salvator ponetur in ea murus et antemurale. Ipse namque est fortissima atque tutissima nostra munitio, juxta illud Proverbiorum: Turris fortissima nomen Domini; ad ipsum currit justus, et exaltabitur. Unde super Christum figere gradum, est ejus auxilio fortiter inhærere, totam in eo spem ponere, ab ejus vestigiis non abire, secundum quod scriptum est: Domine, fortitudo mea, et refugium meum, et robur meum in die tribulationis.
paras.en: [[2:1|and fix my foot|Et figam gradum]], that is, I will make steady and set firmly the step of the heart, or its act, [[2:1|upon the tower|super munitionem]] [*munitio*, a fortification or stronghold], that is, the armour, strengthening and defence of the soul, so that I may always be careful to keep my soul fortified, lest it be overcome by the enemies of its salvation, lest it be mastered by sins or passions. For this is why the Apostle warns the Ephesians: [[Eph 6:11|Put you on the armour of God, that you may be able to stand against the deceits of the devil.|Induite vos armaturam Dei, ut possitis stare adversus insidias diaboli:]] Or, [[2:1|fix my foot upon the tower|Figam gradum super munitionem]], that is, upon Christ, of whom we read in Isaias: [[Is 26:1|a saviour, a wall and a bulwark shall be set therein|Salvator ponetur in ea murus et antemurale]]. For he is our strongest and safest stronghold, according to the saying of Proverbs: [[Prov 18:10|The name of the Lord is a strong tower: the just runneth to it, and shall be exalted.|Turris fortissima nomen Domini; ad ipsum currit justus, et exaltabitur.]] Hence to fix one's foot upon Christ is to cleave strongly to his help, to put all one's hope in him, not to depart from his footsteps, according as it is written: [[Jer 16:19|O Lord, my might, and my strength, and my refuge in the day of tribulation|Domine, fortitudo mea, et refugium meum, et robur meum in die tribulationis]].

paras.t: Et contemplabor, id est, actui rationis ero intentus, ut videam, id est intelligam, quid dicatur mihi, id est, quid Deus in Scripturis mihi præcipiat, quid hortetur, quid consulat, quid etiam vicarii ejus, puta prælati et doctores, mandent et prædicent. Audiam quoque quid loquatur in me Dominus Deus per se, vel per angelicum spiritum. Hinc in Proverbiis habetur: Audi, fili mi, disciplinam; siquidem audiens sapiens, sapientior erit, et intelligens, gubernacula possidebit. Et quid respondeam ad arguentem me, id est quam Deo judici rationem daturus sim in die judicii mei particularis, et etiam universalis. Omnes enim nos manifestari oportet ante tribunal Christi. Felix qui per opera misericordiæ religiosamque vitam, ita quotidie se disponit ad horam divini judicii: qui ut securior Domino occurrat, jam se debet totaliter humiliare, divinæ æquitatis rigorem et suorum defectuum multiplicitatem pensando, juxta quod scriptum est: Non justificabitur homo compositus Deo; et si voluerit cum eo contendere, non poterit respondere unum pro mille. Ideo loquitur Ezechias: Domine, vim patior, responde pro me: quid dicam, aut quid respondebo, quum ipse fecerim?
paras.en: [[2:1|and I will watch|Et contemplabor]] [literally “I will contemplate”], that is, I will be intent upon the act of reason, [[2:1|to see|ut videam]], that is, to understand, [[2:1|what will be said to me|quid dicatur mihi]], that is, what God commands me in the Scriptures, what he exhorts, what he counsels, and also what his vicars, namely prelates and doctors, enjoin and preach. [[Ps 84:9|I will hear what the Lord God will speak in me|Audiam quoque quid loquatur in me Dominus Deus]], by himself, or through an angelic spirit. Hence it is said in Proverbs: [[Prov 1:8|My son, hear the instruction|Audi, fili mi, disciplinam]]; for a [[Prov 1:5|wise man shall hear, and shall be wiser: and he that understandeth shall possess governments|audiens sapiens, sapientior erit, et intelligens, gubernacula possidebit]] [[2:1|and what I may answer to him that reproveth me|Et quid respondeam ad arguentem me]], that is, what account I am to give to God the judge on the day of my particular judgment, and of the universal one also. For [[2 Cor 5:10|we must all be manifested before the judgment seat of Christ|Omnes enim nos manifestari oportet ante tribunal Christi]]. Happy is he who by works of mercy and a religious life so disposes himself each day for the hour of the divine judgment: and that he may go to meet the Lord more securely, he must humble himself wholly even now, weighing the rigour of the divine justice and the multitude of his own failings, according as it is written: [[Job 9:2|man cannot be justified, compared with God|Non justificabitur homo compositus Deo]]; and [[Job 9:3|If he will contend with him, he cannot answer him one for a thousand|et si voluerit cum eo contendere, non poterit respondere unum pro mille]]. Therefore Ezechias says: [[Is 38:14|Lord, I suffer violence, answer thou for me|Domine, vim patior, responde pro me]]: [[Is 38:15|What shall I say|quid dicam]], or what shall I answer, since I myself have done it? [Denis reads *quid respondebo, quum ipse fecerim*; the Vulgate has “what shall he answer for me, whereas he himself hath done it”].

paras.t: Denique providentia ista custodiendi se ipsum, et advertendi quid Deus loquatur, quid etiam ei respondeatur, præsertim inesse debet principibus ac prælatis: quoniam judicium gravissimum in his qui præsunt, fiet. Nempe quo pluribus præsunt, eo ampliorem sollicitudinem atque formidinem habere jugiter debent, propter divini judicii districtionem. Unde in talium persona loquitur Isaias: Super speculum Domini ego sum, stans jugiter per diem; et super custodiam meam ego sum, stans totis noctibus. Et Jeremias ait: Statue tibi speculum, pone tibi amaritudinem. Hoc est accedere ad cor altum, ut exaltetur Deus.
paras.en: Lastly, this forethought in keeping watch over oneself, and in heeding what God says and what answer is to be made to him, ought to be found above all in princes and prelates: for [[Wis 6:6|a most severe judgment shall be for them that bear rule|judicium gravissimum in his qui præsunt, fiet]]. For the more people they are set over, the greater the care and fear they ought continually to have, because of the strictness of the divine judgment. Hence Isaias speaks in the person of such men: [[Is 21:8|I am upon the watchtower of the Lord, standing continually by day: and I am upon my ward, standing whole nights|Super speculum Domini ego sum, stans jugiter per diem; et super custodiam meam ego sum, stans totis noctibus]]. And Jeremias says: [[Jer 31:21|Set thee up a watchtower, make to thee bitterness|Statue tibi speculum, pone tibi amaritudinem]]. This is to [[Ps 63:7|come to a deep heart|accedere ad cor altum]], that God may be exalted[[Ps 63:8||]].

paras.t: Postremo, secundum Hieronymum, in hoc quod Habacuc ait: Contemplabor quid dicatur mihi, et quid respondeam ad arguentem me, eleganter miroque sensu impatientiam describit humanam, quam in disceptationibus semper habere consuevimus, ut antequam nobis ex adverso aliquis respondeat, et sciamus in quo nos arguet, ad respondendum paremur: ex quo ostenditur, responsionem non rationis esse, sed contentionis. Si enim esset ratio, responsio debuerat exspectari, et sic videri an respondere debuerit, an consentire rationali responsioni.
paras.en: Finally, according to Jerome, in saying [[2:1|I will watch|Contemplabor]] [[2:1|what will be said to me, and what I may answer to him that reproveth me|quid dicatur mihi, et quid respondeam ad arguentem me]], Habacuc describes with elegance and wonderful insight the impatience of men, which we always show in disputes: before anyone on the other side answers us, and before we know on what point he will reprove us, we are getting ready to answer; which shows that the answer comes not from reason but from contentiousness. For if it were reason, the answer ought to have been waited for, and then it would be seen whether one ought to answer it, or to agree with a reasonable answer.

paras.t: Jam dixit Propheta in persona justi se velle attendere quid sibi Dominus loqueretur: mox pius Dominus eidem respondet, Isaia dicente: Ad vocem clamoris tui, statim ut audierit, respondebit tibi. Rursusque Dominus repromittit: Antequam clament, ego exaudiam; adhuc illis loquentibus, ego audiam. Etenim juxta Psalmistam: Desiderium pauperum exaudivit Dominus; præparationem cordis eorum audivit auris tua.
paras.en: The Prophet has now said, in the person of the just man, that he wishes to heed what the Lord would say to him: and at once the loving Lord answers him, as Isaias says: [[Is 30:19|at the voice of thy cry, as soon as he shall hear, he will answer thee|Ad vocem clamoris tui, statim ut audierit, respondebit tibi]]. And again the Lord promises: [[Is 65:24|before they call, I will hear; as they are yet speaking, I will hear|Antequam clament, ego exaudiam; adhuc illis loquentibus, ego audiam]]. For according to the Psalmist: [[Ps 9:38|The Lord hath heard the desire of the poor: thy ear hath heard the preparation of their heart.|Desiderium pauperum exaudivit Dominus; præparationem cordis eorum audivit auris tua:]] [the margin gives Ps. x, 17, by the Hebrew numbering; in the Vulgate this is Ps 9:38].

paras.t: Itaque subditur: Et respondit mihi Dominus per inspirationem internam, vel alio modo jam tacto: Scribe visum, et explana eum, id est, instructionem ac revelationem divinam tibi infusam, clare ac lucide imprime, super tabulas, id est in membranis, seu aptis memoriis, pro aliorum et futurorum informatione. Unde Symmachus transtulit, Super paginas. Hinc in Ecclesiastico dicitur: Sapientiam scribe in tempore vacuitatis. Vel, Super tabulas, id est in mentibus hominum, prout in Proverbiis Salomon: Describe, inquit, super latitudinem cordis tui. Apostolus quoque ad Corinthios: Epistola nostra vos estis, scripta in cordibus nostris, non atramento, sed Spiritu Dei viventis, non in tabulis lapideis, sed in tabulis cordis carnalibus. Ut percurrat, id est, expedite atque faciliter sine difficultatis obstaculo intelligat, qui legerit eum, videlicet visum præfatum, puta revelationem tibi factam, cur in hoc mundo impii opprimant justos.
paras.en: So it follows: [[2:2|And the Lord answered me|Et respondit mihi Dominus]], by an inward inspiration, or in the other way already touched on: [[2:2|Write the vision, and make it plain|Scribe visum, et explana eum]], that is, set down clearly and plainly the divine instruction and revelation poured into thee, [[2:2|upon tables|super tabulas]], that is, on parchments, or in fitting records, for the instruction of others and of those to come. Hence Symmachus translated, “upon pages.” Hence it is said in Ecclesiasticus: Write wisdom in the time of leisure[[Ecclus 38:25||]] [Denis reads *scribe*, “write”, where the Vulgate has *scribæ*: “The wisdom of a scribe cometh by his time of leisure”]. Or, [[2:2|upon tables|Super tabulas]], that is, in the minds of men, as Solomon says in Proverbs: Write, he says, upon the breadth of thy heart[[Prov 3:3||]] [Denis's wording follows the older Latin from the Septuagint; the Douay-Rheims has “write them in the tables of thy heart”; cf. Prov 7:3]. The Apostle also, to the Corinthians: [[2 Cor 3:2|You are our epistle, written in our hearts|Epistola nostra vos estis, scripta in cordibus nostris]], [[2 Cor 3:3|not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God: not in tables of stone but in the fleshly tables of the heart|non atramento, sed Spiritu Dei viventis, non in tabulis lapideis, sed in tabulis cordis carnalibus]]. [[2:2|may run over it|Ut percurrat]], that is, may understand it readily and easily, with no difficulty in the way, [[2:2|he that readeth it|qui legerit eum]], namely the aforesaid vision, that is, the revelation made to thee of why in this world the wicked oppress the just.

paras.t: Quia adhuc visus procul, id est, non mox per experientiam innotescet ratio cur Deus permittat improbos et tyrannos in sæculo isto florere ac prævalere; et apparebit in finem, id est, finaliter, tempore divinitus præordinato, patebit causa istius, præsertim in die judicii, vel etiam dum tales a Deo in præsenti vita juste plagantur; et non mentietur, id est, visus prædictus falsus non erit. Istud enim permittitur, ut electi in vita hac a suis peccatis purgentur, majori gratia impleantur, et gloriam ampliorem adipiscantur. Si moram fecerit, exspecta eum, id est, prædicti visus adimpletionem longanimiter præstolare, vel etiam Christi adventum: qui in primo suo adventu edocuit cur Deus prædicta permittat, et in secundo suo adventu per experientiam edocebit quam utile fuerit bonis persecutionem ferre malorum. Hoc quippe tunc declarabit, impios æternaliter condemnando, et electos plenissime glorificando. Quia veniens veniet ipse Christus, itemque visus præinducti impletio, et non tardabit ultra tempus divinitus præstitutum. Nam etsi dilatio adventus Christi atque præfatæ impletionis jam longa appareat, tamen per comparationem futuræ æternitatis, brevissima est. Ideo Petrus archiapostolus ait: Non tardat Dominus promissum. Et in Jacobo legitur: Patientes estote usque ad adventum Domini; et confirmate corda vestra, quoniam adventus Domini appropinquabit: ecce judex ante januam adsistit. Sed et in Apocalypsi Dominus protestatur: Ecce venio cito, et merces mea mecum est, dare unicuique juxta opera sua. Nemo ergo frangatur adversis, sed plenissima spe Deo innitens, veraciter dicat: Etiam si occiderit me, in ipso sperabo. Patientia quippe opus perfectum habet.
paras.en: [[2:3|For as yet the vision is far off|Quia adhuc visus procul]], that is, the reason why God allows the wicked and tyrants to flourish and prevail in this world will not soon become known by experience; [[2:3|and it shall appear at the end|et apparebit in finem]], that is, in the end, at the time ordained by God, the cause of this will be made plain, above all on the day of judgment, or even when such men are justly struck by God in this present life; [[2:3|and shall not lie|et non mentietur]], that is, the aforesaid vision will not be false. For this is allowed so that the elect may be purged of their sins in this life, be filled with greater grace, and gain a fuller glory. [[2:3|if it make any delay, wait for it|Si moram fecerit, exspecta eum]], that is, await with long patience the fulfilment of the aforesaid vision, or else the coming of Christ: who at his first coming taught why God allows these things, and at his second coming will teach by experience how profitable it was for the good to bear the persecution of the wicked. For he will make this plain then, by condemning the wicked for ever and glorifying the elect most fully. [[2:3|for it shall surely come|Quia veniens veniet]], namely Christ himself, and likewise the fulfilment of the vision set out above, [[2:3|and it shall not be slack|et non tardabit]] beyond the time fixed by God. For though the delay of Christ's coming, and of the aforesaid fulfilment, seems long already, yet compared with the eternity to come it is very short. Therefore Peter, the chief of the Apostles, says: [[2 Pet 3:9|The Lord delayeth not his promise|Non tardat Dominus promissum]]. And in James we read: [[Jas 5:7|Be patient|Patientes estote]] [[Jas 5:7|until the coming of the Lord|usque ad adventum Domini]]; and [[Jas 5:8|strengthen your hearts: for the coming of the Lord is at hand|confirmate corda vestra, quoniam adventus Domini appropinquabit]]: [[Jas 5:9|Behold the judge standeth before the door|ecce judex ante januam adsistit]]. And in the Apocalypse too the Lord declares: [[Apoc 22:12|Behold, I come quickly: and my reward is with me, to render to every, man according to his works|Ecce venio cito, et merces mea mecum est, dare unicuique juxta opera sua]]. Let no one, then, be broken by adversity, but leaning on God with the fullest hope, let him say in truth: [[Job 13:15|Although he should kill me, I will trust in him|Etiam si occiderit me, in ipso sperabo]]. For [[Jas 1:4|patience hath a perfect work|Patientia quippe opus perfectum habet]].

paras.t: Et quoniam ipsemet Deus veritas prima locutus est ista, recte subjungitur: Ecce qui incredulus est hujus promissionis divinæ, non erit recta anima ejus in semetipso. Justus autem ex fide sua vivet. Hoc in præcedenti articulo satis tractatum est.
paras.en: And since God himself, the first Truth, has spoken these things, it is rightly added: [[2:4|Behold, he that is unbelieving|Ecce qui incredulus est]] of this divine promise, [[2:4|his soul shall not be right in himself|non erit recta anima ejus in semetipso]]. [[2:4|but the just shall live in his faith|Justus autem ex fide sua vivet]] [the edition notes the reading *in fide* beside *ex fide*]. This has been treated enough in the preceding article.

paras.t: Pro eo quod hic dicitur secundum translationem Hieronymi, Justus ex fide sua vivet, Septuaginta transtulerunt, Justus ex fide mea vivet; sicque Apostolus ad Romanos scripturam istam allegat. Sensus enim est idem, quoniam eadem fides est nostra tanquam subjecti ac recipientis, et Dei tanquam objecti ac influentis.
paras.en: Where it says here, in Jerome's translation, [[2:4|the just shall live in his faith|Justus ex fide sua vivet]], the Septuagint translated, “The just shall live by my faith”; and so the Apostle cites this scripture to the Romans. For the sense is the same, since the same faith is ours as of the subject who receives it, and God's as of the object who pours it in.

paras.t: Et quomodo vinum potantem decipit, id est, suo sapore, candore atque vigore ad deceptionem materialiter occasionaliterque inducit, quamvis potator a propria concupiscentia et gulositate fallatur active atque directe. Decipit autem vinum potantem, quoniam lumen discretionis obtenebrat, et stulto similem facit, ac facile deceptibilem reddit, sicut in Osee habitum est: Fornicatio, et ebrietas, et vinum auferunt cor. Sic erit vir superbus: quia a propria elatione excæcatur et fallitur, putans se aliquid esse, quum nihil sit; ab aliis quoque se putans sapientem et magnum censeri, quum frequenter contingat oppositum: imo multoties a cunctis ejus superbiam considerantibus, deridetur ac spernitur, secundum quod in Ecclesiastico legitur: Odibilis coram Deo et hominibus est superbia; quid superbit terra et cinis? Et non decorabitur, donis gratiæ in præsenti, nec donis gloriæ in futuro: qui enim se exaltat, humiliabitur. Nam et ipsa superbia coram Deo turpissima est, et animam dæmoni specialiter similat. Ideo in Proverbiis Dominus asserit: Arrogantiam et superbiam et os bilingue detestor. Qui dilatavit quasi infernus animam suam, id est, insatiabilis ambitionis cupiditatisque fuit, immoderatissime appetendo honores atque divitias mundi; et ipse quasi mors, et non adimpletur: id est, quemadmodum infernus non adimpletur damnatis, nec mors defunctis, sed omnes consumit et perimit, prout Salomon in Proverbiis scribit, Quatuor sunt insatiabilia, ignis, mors, infernus, etc.; ita superbus non quietatur in divitiis ac mundi honoribus. Appetitum namque rationalis creaturæ caduca ista nequeunt satiare. Et congregabit ad se omnes gentes, id est, diversis et plurimis præesse et dominari conabitur, sicut videmus in multis. Quod totum ad diabolum et Antichristum præcipue potest referri.
paras.en: [[2:5|And as wine deceiveth him that drinketh it|Et quomodo vinum potantem decipit]], that is, by its taste, its brightness and its strength it leads him on to be deceived, materially and as the occasion, although the drinker is deceived actively and directly by his own desire and gluttony. And wine deceives the drinker because it darkens the light of discernment, makes him like a fool, and renders him easy to deceive, as was said in Osee: [[Osee 4:11|Fornication, and wine, and drunkenness, take away the understanding.|Fornicatio, et ebrietas, et vinum auferunt cor]] [[2:5|so shall the proud man be|Sic erit vir superbus]]: for he is blinded and deceived by his own pride, thinking himself to be something when he is nothing; thinking too that others hold him wise and great, when the opposite often happens: indeed many times he is mocked and despised by all who observe his pride, according as we read in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 10:7|Pride is hateful before God and men|Odibilis coram Deo et hominibus est superbia]]; [[Ecclus 10:9|Why is earth, and ashes proud?|quid superbit terra et cinis?]] [[2:5|and he shall not be honoured|Et non decorabitur]] with the gifts of grace in the present, nor with the gifts of glory in the future: for [[Luke 14:11|that exalteth himself shall be humbled|qui enim se exaltat, humiliabitur]][[Luke 18:14||]]. For pride itself is most foul before God, and makes the soul especially like the devil. Therefore the Lord declares in Proverbs: [[Prov 8:13|I hate arrogance, and pride|Arrogantiam et superbiam]], [[Prov 8:13|and a mouth with a double tongue|et os bilingue detestor]]. [[2:5|who hath enlarged his desire like hell|Qui dilatavit quasi infernus animam suam]], that is, he was of an insatiable ambition and greed, seeking the honours and riches of the world beyond all measure; [[2:5|and is himself like death, and he is never satisfied|et ipse quasi mors, et non adimpletur]]: that is, as hell is not filled with the damned, nor death with the dead, but they consume and destroy all, as Solomon writes in Proverbs, There are four things that are never satisfied, fire, death, hell, etc.[[Prov 30:15||]][[Prov 30:16||]] [Denis quotes loosely; Proverbs names hell, the womb, the earth and fire]; so the proud man finds no rest in riches and the honours of the world. For these perishing things cannot satisfy the desire of a rational creature. [[2:5|but will gather together unto him all nations|Et congregabit ad se omnes gentes]], that is, he will strive to be set over and to rule many and various peoples, as we see in many. All this can be referred above all to the devil and to Antichrist.

paras.t: Numquid non omnes isti super eum sument parabolam? Utique omnes electi a superbo quocumque damnato oppressi, quum ejus justam damnationem perspexerint, proverbium quoddam formabunt de eo ex zelo justitiæ, conformantes se æquitati divinæ, et dicent: Væ ei qui multiplicat non sua, id est, justa damnatio nunc infligitur arroganti, qui honorem Deo debitum, aliorumque bona sibi nequiter usurpavit. Hinc de populo reprobo Deus frequenter ait per Jeremiam: Dabo eos in maledictionem, et in proverbium, et in opprobrium, et in sibilum. Quod autem impii in die judicii ab electis taliter irridebuntur, tangitur in Job: Innocens subsannabit eos; et in Psalmo, Lætabitur justus quum viderit vindictam. Usquequo aggravat contra se densum lutum? id est, quamdiu superbus et cupidus in sæculo isto, cœlestibus bonis spiritualibusque animæ divitiis spretis, colligit sibi terrenas divitias, affectum deorsum prementes, et usque ad inferos pertrahentes? quæ animam eas amantem fortiter tenent, et vehementer commaculant, quemadmodum qui denso luto infigitur, non faciliter inde extrahitur, multumque sordidatur. Secundum Hieronymum, divitiæ multiplicatæ, eleganter luto sunt comparatæ, quia in veritate viles sunt et spernendæ, graves, et curis atque distractionibus plenæ. Unde a viris perfectis ut stercora contemnuntur. Et sicut aqua terræ mixta, efficit lutum; sic concupiscentia (quæ comparatur aquæ, juxta illud in Genesi, quod Jacob ad Ruben incestuosum ait: Sicut aqua effusus es) conjuncta terrenis, facit amorem terrenorum, qui est animæ lutum vilissimum. Vilipendenda sunt ergo temporalia et terrena, ut spiritualibus donis ditemur: quibus tanto amplius adimplemur, quo pro Dei amore et gloria cordialius sensibilia atque carnalia aspernamur. Qui enim volunt divites fieri, incidunt in tentationem laqueumque diaboli. Ideo secundum Scripturam, Avaro nihil est scelestius. Et nonne mirum, quod eatenus excæcamur, ut diligentius exquiramus divitias corporis, quam opulentiam animæ, puta virtutes et dona Spiritus Sancti?
paras.en: [[2:6|Shall not all these take up a parable against him|Numquid non omnes isti super eum sument parabolam?]]? Yes indeed: all the elect who were oppressed by any proud man now damned, when they behold his just damnation, will frame a kind of proverb about him out of zeal for justice, conforming themselves to the divine justice, and will say: [[2:6|Woe to him that heapeth together that which is not his own|Væ ei qui multiplicat non sua]], that is, a just damnation is now inflicted on the arrogant man, who wickedly usurped for himself the honour due to God and the goods of others. Hence God often says through Jeremias of the reprobate people: I will give them up to be a curse, and a proverb, and a reproach, and a hissing[[Jer 24:9||]][[Jer 29:18||]] [the words are gathered from these and other places of Jeremias, as the margin's “etc.” shows]. And that the wicked will be so derided by the elect on the day of judgment is touched on in Job: [[Job 22:19|the innocent shall laugh them to scorn|Innocens subsannabit eos]]; and in the Psalm, [[Ps 57:11|The just shall rejoice when he shall see the revenge|Lætabitur justus quum viderit vindictam]]. [[2:6|how long also doth he load himself with thick clay|Usquequo aggravat contra se densum lutum?]]? that is, how long does the proud and greedy man in this world, despising the heavenly goods and spiritual riches of the soul, gather to himself earthly riches, which press the affections downward and drag them down even to hell? These hold fast the soul that loves them and defile it greatly, just as one who is stuck in thick mud is not easily drawn out of it, and is much soiled. According to Jerome, riches heaped up are aptly compared to mud, because in truth they are vile and to be despised, heavy, and full of cares and distractions. Hence perfect men scorn them as dung. And as water mixed with earth makes mud, so desire (which is compared to water, according to what Jacob says in Genesis to the incestuous Ruben: [[Gen 49:4|Thou art poured out as water|Sicut aqua effusus es]]), joined to earthly things, makes the love of earthly things, which is the vilest mud of the soul. Temporal and earthly things are therefore to be held cheap, that we may be enriched with spiritual gifts: and we are filled with these the more abundantly, the more heartily we spurn the things of sense and of the flesh for the love and glory of God. For [[1 Tim 6:9|they that will become rich fall into temptation and into the snare of the devil|Qui enim volunt divites fieri, incidunt in tentationem laqueumque diaboli]]. Therefore, according to the Scripture, [[Ecclus 10:9|nothing is more wicked than the covetous man|Avaro nihil est scelestius]]. And is it not a wonder that we are so far blinded as to seek more diligently the riches of the body than the wealth of the soul, that is, the virtues and the gifts of the Holy Ghost?

paras.t: Numquid non repente consurgent qui mordeant te? id est, iniquitas tua cito punietur, et tu ipse peribis. Punitores autem possunt intelligi dæmones, qui sunt serpentes mordentes. Hinc in Deuteronomio scribitur: Dominus Deus ipse est fortis, et reddens odientibus se statim, ita ut disperdat eos, et ultra non differat, protinus eis restituens quod merentur. Et in Ecclesiastico: Ira a Deo cito approximat; et, Subito veniet ira ejus. Nec obstat quod Salomon profitetur, Etenim quia non cito profertur contra malos judicium, absque ullo timore filii hominum perpetrant mala: quamvis enim interdum videatur divinæ ultio æquitatis diu differri, nihilo minus respectu pœnæ futuræ, vix momentanea comprobatur. Et suscitabuntur lacerantes te, id est, dæmones te acriter affligentes, ad tui punitionem Deo judice provocabuntur, et eris in rapinam eis, quando in manus eorum traderis. Reprobi namque fiunt dæmonum prædæ, dum in eorum captivitatem male vivendo, aut debitas pœnas recipiendo, rediguntur. Ideo Christus in Evangelio peccatores appellat vasa et spolia dæmonis. Et evigilabunt insidiatores tui, id est, hostes præmemorati diligentissimi erunt ad pertrahendum te in loca pœnalia. Diabolus namque tanquam leo rugiens circuit, quærens quem devoret. Dæmones equidem quasi dormiunt et quiescunt, dum nos impugnare, tentare, et tribulare desistunt. Sed quum Deo permittente aut imperante, de novo invadunt, vel ad inferos trahunt, quasi evigilant.
paras.en: [[2:7|Shall they not rise up suddenly that shall bite thee|Numquid non repente consurgent qui mordeant te]]? that is, thy iniquity will soon be punished, and thou thyself shalt perish. The punishers can be understood as the demons, who are biting serpents. Hence it is written in Deuteronomy: The Lord God himself is strong[[Deut 7:9||]], [[Deut 7:10|And repaying forthwith them that hate him, so as to destroy them, without further delay immediately rendering to them what they deserve|et reddens odientibus se statim, ita ut disperdat eos, et ultra non differat, protinus eis restituens quod merentur]]. And in Ecclesiasticus: Wrath cometh quickly from God[[Ecclus 5:7||]]; and, [[Ecclus 5:9|his wrath shall come on a sudden|Subito veniet ira ejus]]. Nor is it against this that Solomon declares: [[Eccles 8:11|For because sentence is not speedily pronounced against the evil, the children of men commit evils without any fear|Etenim quia non cito profertur contra malos judicium, absque ullo timore filii hominum perpetrant mala]]: for though the vengeance of the divine justice sometimes seems long put off, yet compared with the punishment to come it proves to be scarcely a moment. [[2:7|and they be stirred up that shall tear thee|Et suscitabuntur lacerantes te]], that is, the demons who afflict thee sharply will be called forth by God the judge to punish thee, [[2:7|and thou shalt be a spoil to them|et eris in rapinam eis]], when thou art handed over into their hands. For the reprobate become the prey of the demons, when they are brought into their captivity by living evilly, or by receiving the punishments they deserve. This is why Christ in the Gospel calls sinners the vessels and spoils of the devil[[Luke 11:22||]]. And thy liers in wait shall awake[[2:7||]] [these words are not in the Vulgate of Habacuc; they come from the Septuagint, as Jerome gives it], that is, the enemies mentioned above will be most diligent to drag thee away to the places of punishment. For [[1 Pet 5:8|the devil, as a roaring lion, goeth about seeking whom he may devour|Diabolus namque tanquam leo rugiens circuit, quærens quem devoret]]. The demons, indeed, as it were sleep and rest while they cease to attack, tempt and trouble us; but when, by God's leave or command, they invade anew, or drag men to hell, they as it were awake.

paras.t: Quia tu spoliasti gentes multas, bona earum diripiendo, spoliabunt te omnes qui reliqui fuerint de populis, id est, universi electi, qui sunt reliquiæ Dei, in die judicii te condemnabunt, et bonis gloriæ privandum censebunt, sententiam Judicis approbando. Sancti enim judicabunt nationes, et dominabuntur populis. De quibus fertur in Psalmo: Gladii ancipites in manibus eorum, ad faciendam vindictam in nationibus, increpationes in populis, ut faciant in eis judicium conscriptum. Hæc igitur patieris propter sanguinem hominis, id est occisionem eorum quos spiritualiter malo exemplo, persuasione pestifera, comminatione, adulatione aut simili modo necasti, vel corporaliter occidisti sive læsisti, et iniquitatem terræ civitatis, id est propter peccata quæ contra Ecclesiam (quæ est civitas Dei, in terra hac militans) commisisti, et hominum habitantium in ea, id est et propter excessus tuos contra Christifideles, qui fide, caritate, et opere in Ecclesia permanent, ab ecclesiastica unitate atque individua caritate non recedentes.
paras.en: [[2:8|Because thou hast spoiled many nations|Quia tu spoliasti gentes multas]], by plundering their goods, [[2:8|all that shall be left of the people shall spoil thee|spoliabunt te omnes qui reliqui fuerint de populis]], that is, all the elect, who are God's remnant, will condemn thee on the day of judgment and judge that thou art to be deprived of the goods of glory, approving the sentence of the Judge. For the saints [[Wis 3:8|shall judge nations, and rule over people|judicabunt nationes, et dominabuntur populis]]. Of whom it is said in the Psalm: [[Ps 149:6|two-edged swords in their hands|Gladii ancipites in manibus eorum]], [[Ps 149:7|To execute vengeance upon the nations, chastisements among the people|ad faciendam vindictam in nationibus, increpationes in populis]], [[Ps 149:9|To execute upon them the judgment that is written|ut faciant in eis judicium conscriptum]]. These things, then, thou shalt suffer [[2:8|because of men's blood|propter sanguinem hominis]], that is, for the slaying of those whom thou hast killed spiritually by bad example, by pestilent persuasion, by threats, by flattery or in some like way, or whom thou hast killed or harmed in the body, [[2:8|and for the iniquity of the land, of the city|et iniquitatem terræ civitatis]], that is, for the sins thou hast committed against the Church (which is the city of God, militant in this land), [[2:8|and of all that dwell therein|et hominum habitantium in ea]] [Denis reads *hominum*, “of the men”, where the Vulgate has *omnium*], that is, and for thy outrages against the faithful of Christ, who abide in the Church by faith, charity and works, not departing from the unity of the Church and from undivided charity.

paras.t: Væ qui congregat avaritiam malam domui suæ, id est avaro, qui terrena sibi et pueris suis atque familiæ immoderanter periculoseque colligit, ut sit in excelso nidus ejus, id est in sæculo isto sublimiter habitatione et loco, amans primum locum ubique. Multi namque avaritiam ad excellentiam ordinant. Et liberari se putat de manu mali, id est de potestate diaboli, et rigore futuri supplicii. Tales sunt sæculi amatores, qui temporalibus sic inhærent, quod damnationem eis imminentem non pensant neque verentur, sed vana securitate perdunt se ipsos. De quibus ait Apostolus: Quum dixerint, Pax et securitas, tunc repentinus eis superveniet interitus. In Isaia quoque Dominus ait: Veniet super te malum atque calamitas, et nescies ortum eorum. Porro secundum Hieronymum, hoc loco dicitur avaritia mala, ad distinctionem bonæ, ut sit bona avaritia doctoris ecclesiastici, qui nunquam satiatur multitudine sectatorum: et quanto plures habuerit discipulos, tanto magis ad doctrinæ studium concitetur. Unde bona avaritia, est incessabilis appetitus spiritualium divitiarum: quemadmodum bona superbia nuncupatur, qua quis vilitatem peccati detestans, veram Deoque placitam excellentiam cupit. De qua Dominus ait per Isaiam: Ponam te in superbiam sæculorum. Hinc justus, cujus est auxilium a Domino, ascensiones in corde suo disposuit in valle lacrimarum.
paras.en: [[2:9|Woe to him that gathereth together an evil covetousness to his house|Væ qui congregat avaritiam malam domui suæ]] [*avaritia*, “covetousness” or “avarice”], that is, woe to the covetous man, who gathers earthly goods for himself, his children and his household beyond measure and to his peril, [[2:9|that his nest may be on high|ut sit in excelso nidus ejus]], that is, that he may dwell loftily in this world in his house and his station, loving the first place everywhere. For many direct their avarice to eminence. [[2:9|and thinketh he may be delivered out of the hand of evil|Et liberari se putat de manu mali]], that is, out of the power of the devil and the rigour of the punishment to come. Such are the lovers of the world, who so cleave to temporal things that they neither weigh nor fear the damnation hanging over them, but destroy themselves by a vain security. Of whom the Apostle says: [[1 Thess 5:3|when they shall say: Peace and security; then shall sudden destruction come upon them|Quum dixerint, Pax et securitas, tunc repentinus eis superveniet interitus]]. In Isaias too the Lord says: [[Is 47:11|Evil shall come upon thee|Veniet super te malum]] and calamity, [[Is 47:11|and thou shalt not know the rising thereof|et nescies ortum eorum]]. Further, according to Jerome, an *evil* covetousness is spoken of here to distinguish it from a good one: so that there is a good avarice in the doctor of the Church, who is never satisfied with the number of his followers, and the more disciples he has, the more he is stirred to the pursuit of teaching. Hence good avarice is an unceasing desire for spiritual riches; just as that is called a good pride by which a man, detesting the baseness of sin, desires a true excellence pleasing to God. Of which the Lord says through Isaias: [[Is 60:15|I will make thee to be an everlasting glory|Ponam te in superbiam sæculorum]] [literally “I will make thee the pride of the ages”, which is Denis's point]. Hence the just man, whose help is from the Lord[[Ps 120:2||]], [[Ps 83:6|in his heart he hath disposed to ascend by steps|ascensiones in corde suo disposuit]] [[Ps 83:7|In the vale of tears|in valle lacrimarum]].

paras.t: Cogitasti confusionem domui tuæ, id est, consensu et mente ea tractasti quæ animum faciunt inordinatum ac vitiosum, confusionemque merentur tibi et pertinentibus ad te consentientibus tibi, imo et damnationem æternam, in qua nullus est ordo, sed summa confusio. Concidisti populos multos, eos corporaliter spiritualiterve lædendo, ut dictum est; et peccavit anima tua, id est tu ipse in eos: ponendo partem pro toto. Cujus peccati indicium est, Quia lapis de pariete clamabit. Hoc intelligi potest, vel de ipsis ædificiis electorum ab impiis dissipatis, secundum intellectum in præcedenti articulo positum, vel de electis, qui sunt lapides vivi ipsius Ecclesiæ, qui sæpe zelo justitiæ clamant ad Deum contra iniquos. Quidam per lapidem istum intelligunt Christum, lapidem angularem, qui in judicio clamat adversus damnandos, juxta illud in Isaia: Vociferabitur et clamabit, et super inimicos suos confortabitur.
paras.en: [[2:10|Thou hast devised confusion to thy house|Cogitasti confusionem domui tuæ]], that is, by consent and in mind thou hast dealt with those things which make the soul disordered and vicious, and which earn confusion for thee and for those belonging to thee who consent to thee, nay, eternal damnation as well, in which there is no order but utter confusion. [[2:10|thou hast cut off many people|Concidisti populos multos]], harming them in body or in soul, as was said; [[2:10|and thy soul hath sinned|et peccavit anima tua]], that is, thou thyself hast sinned against them, the part being put for the whole. The sign of this sin is: [[2:11|For the stone shall cry out of the wall|Quia lapis de pariete clamabit]]. This can be understood either of the very buildings of the elect pulled down by the wicked, according to the sense given in the preceding article, or of the elect, who are the living stones of the Church itself, who often cry to God against the wicked out of zeal for justice.
